masthead_title: Credit finally joined today's stock selloff — the first time in over a week that rates, credit, the dollar, and stocks have all leaned the same tightening direction at once.
regime_line: Both HY and IG OAS widened back above their own flag lines today (z +1.85 and +1.79) right alongside a stock selloff that pushed the S&P 500 (−1.03%) and Russell 2000 (−1.50%) into their own flags too, while the 10-year Treasury held at 5.10%, a level that's been here on 23 of the last 38 sessions and, before this run, was last reached in July 2007.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — two confirmed

  • CL-0069 (Friday's chip/AI-hardware reversal as a resumption of the Nov. 5 AI-capex-doubt selloff, due 2026-11-19) — confirmed, two sessions early. SMH closed below Friday's $486.75 reference on both sessions since (Monday $461.90, Tuesday $460.10) — already two of the three sessions the test needed, and SMH never came close to the $500 refute line.
  • CL-0070 (whether the market read Nvidia's after-the-close Q3 earnings — its first since Jensen Huang's Nov. 11 resignation — as deepening the AI-capex doubt or easing it, due today) — confirmed. SMH closed Tuesday at $460.10, below the $461.90 reference and well short of the $486.75 refute line — the doubt deepened into the session itself, hours before Nvidia's own numbers were even known.
story_html:
Tuesday's dominant financial-press narrative was a renewed slide in software stocks, not chips. Salesforce fell about 9% to $194.52, its worst day on this screen, with ServiceNow (−6.5% to $92.90), Workday, Datadog, and Oracle all down alongside it. GuruFocus and Pomegra tied the move to the same AI-disruption-and-monetization doubt that hit chip stocks earlier this month; Yahoo Finance quoted an RBC Capital Markets analyst warning that the AI companies are going to try to take Salesforce's business away entirely, and Pomegra linked the selling to Anthropic's roughly $64 billion IPO, pricing Thursday, pulling capital out of application-software names ahead of it. One outlet, Invezz, separately tied Salesforce's drop to a string of recent technology outages raising software-reliability worries — a claim this morning's search could not corroborate elsewhere, so it is reported single-sourced, not as settled fact. Intuit (−7.2%) and ServiceNow fell with no news of their own — Intuit's own earnings aren't due until Thursday after the close — a pattern of sympathy selling into an unreported earnings date (Unit 6's September lesson, applied live). Separately, after Tuesday's close, Nvidia topped Q3 estimates, announced a $150 billion buyback, and gave a Q4 outlook ahead of consensus — its first report since Jensen Huang's Nov. 11 resignation — and was trading up nearly 4% premarket Wednesday, per CNBC.

This system's own pull backs the press narrative more than it has in weeks. Unlike Monday, when credit stayed flat while equities and chips sold off, both high-yield and investment-grade spreads widened today and are back above their own flag lines (Dashboard, below) — the first time in over a week that credit has moved the same direction as a stock selloff rather than sitting it out. Breadth confirms too: the equal-weight S&P (RSP) fell 1.45%, more than the S&P 500's own 1.03% — a reversal from the narrow, mega-cap-driven selling of the past two weeks (Unit 6's breadth tool, reactivated). Today's decliners ran wide: software (Salesforce, Intuit, ServiceNow), healthcare (UnitedHealth, −5.4%), cell-tower REITs (SBAC and CCI, both off more than 5.8% as real yields climbed — Dashboard, below), and consumer names (Nike, Best Buy). Rates, the dollar, credit, and now breadth are, for the first time in over a week, all leaning the same tightening direction at once — the live case for Unit 8's capstone, below. The S&P 500's 1.03% drop is itself an ordinary-sized move (one this big happens about 33 times a year over the last 30 years, and it's the 24th such day this year; Monday's own 1.9% drop was bigger). It's the number of things agreeing today, not the size of any one of them, that makes this morning worth a second look.
dashboard_interp_html:
Every Treasury tenor eased a touch today, but the front end stayed the dashboard's most flagged corner. The 3-month bill eased 1bp to 4.33% but is still up 9bp over five sessions (z +1.83, flagged; 54th percentile since the early 1980s but the 72nd of the last 30 years). The 2-year eased 3bp to 4.80% but is up 24bp over five sessions (z +1.42, just below the flag line; 53rd percentile over the full 50-year record but the 83rd of the last 30 years, † a 30-point gap). The 10-year eased 2bp to 5.10% (z +1.21, below the flag line; 47th/85th %ile, † today's lead History-check fact, below) and the 30-year held flat at 5.46% (z +1.17; 48th/84th %ile, †). The curve itself barely moved (2s10s +1bp to 30bp; 3m10y −1bp to 77bp, both comfortably un-inverted, neither flagged). Why this matters: every tenor easing slightly on a day stocks fell hard is itself informative — a genuine flight-to-Treasuries bid would have pushed yields down harder than a couple of basis points. This reads as a small pause inside a longer climb, not a reversal: closer to a CD rate holding steady than a mortgage rate actually easing.

Credit, by contrast, didn't just hold — it moved, and it moved with equities. HY OAS (dated Monday 11-16, the usual one-session lag) widened 11bp to 334bp (z +1.85, flagged; 81st percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked *, since this live series has no multi-decade history — see §4F). IG OAS (also dated 11-16) ticked up 1bp to 90bp (z +1.79, flagged; 63rd percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked *). Both tiers of credit easing together was last week's story; both widening together is today's — the first time since late October that credit has leaned the same direction as a stock selloff instead of sitting it out. SOFR (also dated 11-16) rose 3bp to 3.93% (z +1.64, flagged; 45th percentile over the full 72-year record but the 68th of the last 30 years, †). The dollar eased slightly on the day (DXY −0.06 to 103.49) but is still up 1.26 points over five sessions and carries this run's single largest Tier 1 flag (z +2.36; 74th percentile over the full 55-year record but the 84th of the last 30 years, no real gap). The 10-year TIPS real yield (dated Monday) rose 1bp to 2.92%, up 29bp over five sessions (z +1.83, flagged; 99.7th percentile of its own 24-year TIPS record — but the Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, puts real rates at just the 80th percentile of the last 30 years and the 54th since 1982, a materially milder read using the same concept). The 10-year breakeven eased 4bp to 2.20% (z −1.81, flagged; 48th percentile of its own 24-year record, about the middle historically even as it's flagged lately). Why this matters: when credit, the market's own read on default risk, starts moving in the same direction as a stock selloff instead of shrugging it off, that's the signal worth taking most seriously on this page — not because any single number here is extreme, but because the whole hierarchy just started pointing the same way at once.
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is still the 10-year Treasury, at 5.10% after first reaching this level Sep. 23 — there on 23 of 38 sessions since. Before this run, the last time was July 2007; this run's own high, 5.31% on Oct. 5, was last matched in May 2002. The two lenses disagree: the 85th percentile of the last 30 years, but just the 47th of the full 65-year record — unusual lately, unremarkable across the full sweep, since that record folds in the double-digit yields of the late 1970s-80s. The then-vs-now panel pairs today against July 2007: the 10-year lines up almost exactly (5.10% vs. 5.11%), but the policy rate doesn't — fed funds was 5.25% then vs. SOFR's 3.93% now (SOFR: 45th percentile all-time, 68th of the last 30 years).

Second: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.92%, Monday) sits at the 99.7th percentile of its own 24-year record, there on 5 of 32 sessions since Sep. 30. Before this run, last reached November 2008, in the Global Financial Crisis, and only briefly. The Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, reads milder: the 80th percentile of the last 30 years, just the 54th since 1982 — TIPS alone are too short a history to call this extreme on their own.

Third: the 2-year Treasury yield is up 133bp this year — the 9th-largest rise through this date in 50 years (bigger: 2022 +370bp, 1994 +296bp, 1980 +248bp). A 12-month rise this big (1.20 points) has started 8 times since 1977; the S&P 500 was lower a year later in 3 of 8 (any 12-month stretch since 1962: 24.4%), a recession beginning within two years in 2 of 8 (any two-year stretch outside a recession: 27.4%). Client-ready: rates got here fast; speed alone hasn't usually broken markets.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 29 name candidates qualified Tuesday — every one of them a decliner — but no sector ETF cleared the 1.5pp divergence bar, even with the cluster below: dispersion inside tech itself (software down hard, chips flat to down modestly) kept the sector-level average close to the index. Oracle (−3.43%) and Wells Fargo (−2.53%) qualified via the megacap screen rather than the 4% bar. Earnings/guidance reactions are prioritized per §5, but none of today's three largest movers had a company-specific catalyst — all three already reported this quarter. Also qualifying, left out under the cap: SBAC (−6.46%), NKE (−6.30%), FSLR (−5.84%), CCI (−5.82%), WDAY (−5.80%), FICO (−5.68%), UNH (−5.42%), MKC (−5.09%), GPN (−5.01%), GDDY (−4.91%), EFX (−4.86%), FDS (−4.84%), BBY (−4.79%), IBM (−4.71%), TTWO (−4.47%), TPR (−4.45%), DDOG (−4.44%), XYZ (−4.40%), MCO (−4.32%), ADBE (−4.25%), SW (−4.25%), MSCI (−4.20%), SPGI (−4.08%), COIN (−4.02%), ORCL (−3.43%), WFC (−2.53%) — not individually researched today given the cap; none asserted to lack a catalyst, simply not checked.

Salesforce (CRM) −9.45% (194.52, from 214.83) — what happened: the session's largest decliner on this screen, by a wide margin. Stated reason: part of a broad application-software selloff that GuruFocus and Pomegra tied to renewed doubt that AI tools will let incumbent software vendors keep growing as fast as they have; an RBC Capital Markets analyst told Yahoo Finance the AI companies are going to try to take Salesforce's business away entirely. Pomegra also linked the selling to Anthropic's roughly $64 billion IPO, pricing Thursday, pulling investor capital out of application-software names ahead of it. One outlet (Invezz) separately tied part of the move to a string of recent technology outages raising software-reliability worries — a claim this morning's search could not corroborate elsewhere, reported single-sourced, not as settled fact. Read-through: a different node of the same AI-capex debate Tier 3 tracks daily through chips (below) — this time about whether AI disrupts the software incumbents' own revenue, not whether hyperscalers keep spending on infrastructure. → Route to NR commentary process (Flags, below); no position-level view (§8).

Intuit (INTU) −7.17% (320.79, from 345.56) — what happened: the session's second-largest decliner. Stated reason: no company-specific news surfaced; Intuit's own fiscal Q1 earnings aren't due until Thursday (Nov. 19) after the close. GuruFocus and Pomegra describe the drop as part of the same software-sector selloff as Salesforce's. Read-through: sympathy selling into an unreported earnings date — Unit 6's September lesson, applied live — which raises the stakes on Thursday's own print considerably higher than it would have been a week ago.

ServiceNow (NOW) −6.51% (92.90, from 99.37) — what happened: the session's third-largest decliner, and its lowest close since July. Stated reason: 24/7 Wall St. put the stock's cumulative loss at roughly $59 billion over the past 14 trading sessions — a stretch that began with an actual revenue beat — attributing the continued slide to the same sector-wide AI-disruption narrative rather than anything in the company's own numbers. Read-through: a clean, dated illustration of §4C's point about causal narration: an actual beat has been overridden by a sector story for two weeks running, itself evidence this move is sentiment-driven rather than fundamentals-driven for this name specifically. → Route to NR commentary process (Flags, below); no position-level view (§8).

Sector note: no GICS sector ETF cleared the 1.5pp divergence bar today, even with the software cluster above — dispersion inside tech itself kept the sector-level average close to the index. Nothing to report here by the mechanical rule; not the same as nothing moving.

calendar_note_html:
Today: the FOMC's own Meeting Minutes (2:00pm ET) are the day's one high-impact scheduled release; the rest of the calendar is low-impact housing data (Building Permits and Housing Starts, both 8:30am ET) and routine remarks from Fed officials Barr, Williams, and Kashkari.

Why this matters to the current regime: the minutes are from the meeting behind this run's own rate climb (Dashboard, above) — language read as leaning toward holding rates higher for longer would reinforce today's tightening read across rates, credit, and the dollar, while anything read as more dovish would be the first real complication to it. Nvidia's premarket move (Tier 3, above) is the other live thread: a reassuring close into tonight that calms the chip/memory complex would complicate the "AI trade in doubt" framing (Story, above), while giving the gain back would confirm it further. New claim CL-0071 (Flags, below) is built to grade the market's actual read on it by tomorrow morning.
concept_unit: Unit 8 — Cross-asset confirmation, segment 8 (capstone) — curriculum complete
concept_title: When all four votes finally agree — the hierarchy-of-evidence habit, applied end to end, closes the eight-unit curriculum
concept_html:
Segments 1 through 7 built the hierarchy one piece at a time: rates, credit, liquidity, the dollar, breadth, financing structure, and then cross-asset confirmation itself — rates, credit, the dollar, and equities, with commodities folded in as a mostly-dollar echo rather than a fifth independent vote (segment 7). Most days, these votes split: credit shrugs while equities sell off, or the dollar and gold both fall together for the same dollar-pricing reason rather than two separate opinions. Today is the exception that makes the habit useful. Both HY and IG OAS widened alongside the stock selloff for the first time in over a week; breadth broke the same direction too, with the equal-weight S&P falling more than the cap-weighted index for the first time in two weeks (Story, above); the dollar and rates were already leaning tight. Four votes, one direction, on a day whose single biggest number — the S&P's 1.03% drop — is itself unremarkable (a move that size happens about 33 times a year).

That's the whole point of building the habit over eight units: the size of any one number matters less than whether the others agree with it, and today several of them finally did. This closes the curriculum's eight-unit sequence — the dual endpoint from §7 is now in place: reading the data like an analyst (the hierarchy itself) and explaining it like an advisor (the client-translation line below). From here, the brief reinforces these eight tools against live data rather than introducing new ones.
client_translation: When your statement looks rough and the news, the bond market, and credit spreads are all telling the same story at once, that's worth paying more attention to than any one of them alone — even on a day when no single number looks historically dramatic.
client_lens_html:
“Why did Salesforce fall 9% with no earnings?” It wasn't company news — it's part of a broader worry that AI tools could eventually take business away from software companies like Salesforce, not a one-day story. Intuit and ServiceNow fell the same day on the same theme, with no news of their own.

“Is this the same AI selloff as the chip stocks a few weeks ago?” Related, but not identical. The chip selloff was about whether companies keep spending on AI data centers and chips. This week's move is about whether AI tools disrupt the software companies themselves — a different worry, inside the same broad AI-capex debate.

“Should I be more worried this time?” This is the first day in over a week where rates, credit spreads, the dollar, and the stock market have all leaned the same direction together — worth watching, though no individual number today is historically extreme. We'll keep checking whether it holds tomorrow, and into this afternoon's Fed minutes.
